topic: Test techniques and black-box test design

notes.front: What is a test technique?
notes.back: “A procedure used to define test conditions, design test cases, and specify test data.”
notes.explanation: One procedure yields three outputs of test work: the conditions to aim at, the cases built on them and the values those cases feed in.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test technique”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A procedure used to define test conditions, design test cases, and specify test data.
notes.example: Like following a recipe rather than cooking by feel: for a postcode field, a technique tells the tester which groups of values to aim at and which actual values to type.

notes.front: What is a coverage item?
notes.back: “An attribute or combination of attributes derived from one or more test conditions by using a test technique.”
notes.explanation: Applying a technique to a test condition turns it into concrete things a test can be checked against.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “coverage item”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: An attribute or combination of attributes derived from one or more test conditions by using a test technique.
notes.example: Like the stops on a delivery round: from the condition “customer pays by card”, a technique might yield separate items for debit, credit and prepaid cards, each one to be visited.

notes.front: What is coverage?
notes.back: “The degree to which specified coverage items are exercised by a test suite, expressed as a percentage.”
notes.explanation: As a percentage, it shows how much of what a technique identified the tests have actually reached.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “coverage”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The degree to which specified coverage items are exercised by a test suite, expressed as a percentage.
notes.example: Like the progress bar on a to-do app: the share of listed items ticked off, rather than the number of hours worked.

notes.front: What is a black-box test technique?
notes.back: “A test technique based on the specification of a component or system.” It is also called a specification-based technique.
notes.explanation: The tester works from what the test object should do, not from how it is built inside.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “black-box test technique”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test technique based on the specification of a component or system.
notes.example: Like testing a vending machine only by pressing its buttons and checking what drops out, using the label on the front to know what should happen.

notes.front: What is a white-box test technique?
notes.back: “A test technique based on the internal structure of a component or system.” It is also called a structure-based technique.
notes.explanation: The tester designs tests by looking inside, at how the test object is built and how it processes data.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “white-box test technique”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test technique based on the internal structure of a component or system.
notes.example: Like an electrician testing a house by tracing each circuit on the wiring plan, rather than just flicking the switches.

notes.front: What is an experience-based test technique?
notes.back: “A test technique based on the tester's experience, knowledge and intuition.”
notes.explanation: Here the tester's own background, rather than a document or the code, is the main source of test ideas.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “experience-based test technique”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A test technique based on the tester's experience, knowledge and intuition.
notes.example: Like a mechanic who has serviced one car model for years and goes straight to the parts that usually give trouble.

notes.front: What is equivalence partitioning (EP)?
notes.back: “A black-box test technique in which test conditions are equivalence partitions exercised by one representative member of each partition.”
notes.explanation: Rather than testing every value, the tester groups values and lets one member stand for its whole group.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “equivalence partitioning”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A black-box test technique in which test conditions are equivalence partitions exercised by one representative member of each partition.
notes.example: Like tasting one spoonful from each pot on a stove rather than every spoonful: each pot is a group whose contents should all taste the same.

notes.front: In equivalence partitioning, what is a valid partition?
notes.back: A partition made up of valid values, for example values the test object should process.
notes.explanation: Valid partitions hold the values the test object is meant to accept and handle.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like the ticket types a cinema till is built to sell: “adult”, “child” and “senior” could each be a valid partition.

notes.front: In equivalence partitioning, what is an invalid partition?
notes.back: A partition made up of invalid values, for example values the test object should ignore or reject.
notes.explanation: Invalid partitions hold values the test object should turn away, or values whose handling is not defined.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like asking that cinema till for a negative number of tickets: all such requests form one invalid partition.

notes.front: What is Each Choice coverage?
notes.back: A coverage criterion for several sets of partitions: test cases must exercise every partition in every set at least once.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls it the simplest criterion when a test item has more than one set of partitions, such as several input parameters.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like checking that each shirt size and each shirt colour has been ordered at least once during a web shop's test run.

notes.front: What is boundary value analysis (BVA)?
notes.back: “A black-box test technique in which the test conditions are boundary values.”
notes.explanation: It aims tests at the edges of partitions, where one group of values ends and the next begins.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “boundary value analysis”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A black-box test technique in which the test conditions are boundary values.
notes.example: Like checking a lift's overload alarm with a load at exactly its rated limit, rather than at half load.

notes.front: In BVA, what is a boundary value?
notes.back: The minimum or maximum value of an ordered partition.
notes.explanation: These edge values mark where one partition stops and the next starts.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like the first and last house numbers on one side of a street: for a partition of ages 13 to 19, they are 13 and 19.

notes.front: What is 2-value BVA?
notes.back: A form of BVA with two coverage items per boundary value: the boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition.
notes.explanation: Each boundary is tested once from inside its partition and once from just across the edge.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like checking a fence from both sides at one post: for a partition of 13 to 19, its top edge gives 19 and 20.

notes.front: What is 3-value BVA?
notes.back: A form of BVA with three coverage items per boundary value: the boundary value and both its neighbours.
notes.explanation: It adds the neighbour on the inside of the boundary, which need not itself be a boundary value.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like checking a fence post plus one step to each side: for a partition of 13 to 19, its top edge gives 18, 19 and 20.

notes.front: What is decision table testing (DTT)?
notes.back: “A black-box test technique in which the test conditions are the combinations of conditions and the resulting actions shown in a decision table.”
notes.explanation: Each combination of conditions in the table, with the actions it should lead to, becomes something to test.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “decision table testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A black-box test technique in which the test conditions are the combinations of conditions and the resulting actions shown in a decision table.
notes.example: Like an insurer's rate sheet that says which premium applies for each mix of “young driver”, “sports car” and “past claims”.

notes.front: What is state transition testing?
notes.back: “A black-box test technique in which test conditions are state transitions or sequences of them.”
notes.explanation: Tests follow the test object as it moves from one state to another in response to events.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “state transition testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A black-box test technique in which test conditions are state transitions or sequences of them.
notes.example: Like testing a washing machine by taking it from “idle” to “washing” to “spinning” and checking each change of mode.

notes.front: What is a state diagram?
notes.back: A model showing a system's possible states and the valid transitions between them.
notes.explanation: It is the model state transition testing works from: states to reach and transitions to exercise.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a map of a British traffic light: red, then red and amber, then green, then amber, with arrows for the changes allowed.

notes.front: In a state diagram, what is a guard condition?
notes.back: An extra condition that may qualify the event that starts a transition.
notes.explanation: In the usual transition label it sits in square brackets after the event.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a cash machine that pays out on the event “request withdrawal” only when the balance is high enough.

notes.front: What is a state table?
notes.back: A model equivalent to a state diagram: rows are states, columns are events, and cells hold the target state and any actions.
notes.explanation: It carries the same model as the diagram, laid out as a grid.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a mileage chart in a road atlas: find the row for where you are and the column for what happens, and the cell tells you the result.

notes.front: What is all states coverage?
notes.back: A state transition coverage criterion whose coverage items are the states; 100% means every state has been exercised.
notes.explanation: It is measured as the number of exercised states divided by the total number of states, as a percentage.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like visiting every room of a house at least once, whichever doors you happen to use.

notes.front: What is valid transitions coverage?
notes.back: A criterion, also called 0-switch coverage, whose coverage items are single valid transitions; 100% means all of them are exercised.
notes.explanation: It is measured as exercised valid transitions divided by all valid transitions, as a percentage.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like walking through every door of a house that is meant to be used, at least once each.

notes.front: What is all transitions coverage?
notes.back: A criterion whose coverage items are all transitions in a state table: valid ones are exercised and invalid ones attempted.
notes.explanation: Invalid transitions count too, so the tests must also try moves the model does not allow.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like walking through every usable door of a house and also trying each locked one to check it stays shut.

notes.front: What is defect masking?
notes.back: When one defect stops another from being found.
notes.explanation: Tests can look clean for the second defect only because the first one stopped them reaching it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a blown fuse hiding a badly wired socket: with no power reaching the socket, its fault cannot show.

notes.front: Test techniques help with two activities: test analysis, which settles {{c1::what to test}}, and test design, which settles how to test.
notes.back: What to test.
notes.explanation: Analysis and design are the two activities the techniques serve, each answering its own question.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of set of test cases do test techniques help a tester develop?
notes.back: A fairly small but sufficient set, built systematically.
notes.explanation: The aim is enough tests chosen by method, not every test that could be run.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During analysis and design, which three things do test techniques help the tester define or identify?
notes.back: Test conditions, coverage items and test data.
notes.explanation: Each of these is an output a technique produces on the way to finished test cases.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Into which three categories does the syllabus classify test techniques?
notes.back: Black-box, white-box and experience-based.
notes.explanation: Each category draws its tests from a different place: the specification, the internal structure or the tester.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are black-box test cases independent of how the software is implemented?
notes.back: They are based on the specified behaviour of the test object, without reference to its internal structure.
notes.explanation: Code can be rewritten without touching them, as long as the required behaviour stays the same.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When can white-box test cases be created?
notes.back: Only after the design or implementation of the test object exists.
notes.explanation: They depend on how the software is designed, so there must be a design to analyse first.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the effectiveness of experience-based test techniques depend heavily on?
notes.back: The tester's skills.
notes.explanation: The techniques put the tester's knowledge and experience to work, so results vary with who applies them.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why are experience-based techniques called complementary to black-box and white-box techniques?
notes.back: They can detect defects that black-box and white-box techniques may miss.
notes.explanation: They add to the systematic techniques rather than replacing them.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which black-box test techniques does the v4.0.1 syllabus discuss?
notes.back: Four: equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing and state transition testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls these commonly used; each earns its own section and learning objective.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2 Black-Box Test Techniques, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which syllabus black-box technique divides data into groups whose elements are expected to be processed the same way?
notes.back: Equivalence partitioning (EP).
notes.explanation: Its groups, the partitions, rest on that expectation of identical treatment.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which syllabus black-box technique exercises the edges of ordered partitions?
notes.back: Boundary value analysis (BVA).
notes.explanation: It builds on partitions but looks only at their minimum and maximum values.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which syllabus black-box technique records combinations of conditions and the actions they lead to?
notes.back: Decision table testing.
notes.explanation: Its table lists the conditions and actions as rows and each combination as a column.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which syllabus black-box technique models the states of a system and the events that move it between them?
notes.back: State transition testing.
notes.explanation: Its tests are sequences of events that drive the system from state to state.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which black-box technique from the 2018 Foundation syllabus was removed in v4.0?
notes.back: Use case testing. It is still in the Advanced Test Analyst syllabus.
notes.explanation: Older study material may still teach it, but it is no longer part of the Foundation syllabus.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 10 Appendix C – Release Notes, p. 75
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What expectation is equivalence partitioning based on?
notes.back: That all the elements of a given partition will be processed in the same way by the test object.
notes.explanation: If the test object treats a whole group alike, one member can speak for the group.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In equivalence partitioning, {{c1::one test}} for each partition is considered sufficient.
notes.back: One test.
notes.explanation: Every value in a partition is expected to reveal the same defects, so extra values from it add nothing new.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides inputs, what are two other kinds of data element that equivalence partitions can be identified for?
notes.back: Any two of, among others: outputs, configuration items, internal values, time-related values and interface parameters.
notes.explanation: EP applies to any data element related to the test object, not only to what a user enters.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two pairs of opposite properties that equivalence partitions may have?
notes.back: Any two of: continuous or discrete; ordered or unordered; finite or infinite.
notes.explanation: EP is not limited to number ranges; a partition may equally be an unordered or infinite set.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: No value may sit in two equivalence partitions at once: partitions must not {{c1::overlap}}, and none may be empty.
notes.back: Overlap.
notes.explanation: Together, the two rules make each partition a distinct group with at least one value to test.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does the syllabus say partitioning should be done with care?
notes.back: In practice, understanding how the test object will treat different values is often complicated.
notes.explanation: The syllabus grants that EP can be easy for simple test items, but real ones often are not simple.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Do all teams define valid and invalid values in the same way?
notes.back: No; the definitions of valid and invalid values may vary among teams and organisations.
notes.explanation: The syllabus offers more than one reading of each word rather than a single fixed definition.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two ways a team may interpret “valid values”?
notes.back: Values the test object should process, or values whose processing the specification defines.
notes.explanation: One reading looks at intended behaviour, the other at what the specification actually covers.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two ways a team may interpret “invalid values”?
notes.back: Values the test object should ignore or reject, or values for which the specification defines no processing.
notes.explanation: As with valid values, one reading looks at intended behaviour and the other at the specification's gaps.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In equivalence partitioning, what are the coverage items?
notes.back: The equivalence partitions.
notes.explanation: Coverage therefore counts groups reached, not the number of values or tests.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: 100% EP coverage needs at least one test in every identified partition, {{c1::the invalid partitions included}}.
notes.back: The invalid partitions included.
notes.explanation: Groups of values the test object should reject are still partitions, so they count towards the total.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is EP coverage measured?
notes.back: Partitions exercised by at least one test case, divided by the total number of identified partitions, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: A partition counts once however many tests touch it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When a test item has several sets of partitions, for example several input parameters, what does one test case cover?
notes.back: Partitions from different sets of partitions at once.
notes.explanation: A single test supplies a value for every parameter, so it touches one partition in each set.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does Each Choice coverage take combinations of partitions into account?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Its only demand is that every partition of every set is exercised at least once, in whatever pairing.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why can BVA be used only for ordered partitions?
notes.back: It is based on exercising the boundaries of equivalence partitions, and boundaries need ordered values.
notes.explanation: An unordered set, such as a list of names, has no lowest or highest member to test.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For BVA, a partition must have no gaps: any value lying {{c1::between}} two members of a partition belongs to it too.
notes.back: Between.
notes.explanation: Each partition is then an unbroken stretch of values with one lowest and one highest member.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does BVA focus on boundary values?
notes.back: Developers are more likely to make errors with boundary values.
notes.explanation: Tests go where the syllabus says errors are most likely, rather than into the middle of a partition.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where are the typical defects found by BVA located?
notes.back: Where the code puts a boundary too high or too low, or leaves it out entirely.
notes.explanation: Each is a mistake in where the code puts the edge of a partition.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many versions of BVA does the v4.0.1 syllabus cover, and how do they differ?
notes.back: Two, 2-value and 3-value BVA, which differ in the number of coverage items per boundary needed for 100% coverage.
notes.explanation: The same boundaries are used; only the number of values tested around each one changes.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is 2-value BVA coverage measured?
notes.back: Boundary values exercised, divided by the total number of identified boundary values, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: The closest neighbour lies in the adjacent partition, where it is that partition's own boundary value, so every item counted is a boundary value.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is 3-value BVA coverage measured?
notes.back: Boundary values and their neighbours exercised, divided by the total of identified boundary values and their neighbours, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: The neighbours are counted separately because some of them are not boundary values.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In 3-value BVA, some coverage items {{c1::may not be boundary values}}.
notes.back: May not be boundary values.
notes.explanation: The extra neighbour sits inside the same partition, where it need not be an edge.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which is more rigorous, 2-value or 3-value BVA?
notes.back: 3-value BVA, as it may detect defects that 2-value BVA overlooks.
notes.explanation: Its extra value on the inside of each boundary checks more than the edge and the value beyond it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of requirements are decision tables used to test the implementation of?
notes.back: Requirements where the outcome depends on which combination of conditions holds.
notes.explanation: The table lays out each combination so that its outcome can be checked.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of logic are decision tables an effective way of recording?
notes.back: Complex logic, such as business rules.
notes.explanation: A grid of conditions and actions keeps many interacting rules readable.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a decision table, what forms the rows?
notes.back: The conditions and the resulting actions of the system.
notes.explanation: Conditions and actions are defined first, then combined column by column.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a decision table, what does each column correspond to?
notes.back: A decision rule: a unique combination of conditions, with its associated actions.
notes.explanation: Reading down a column gives one complete “if these, then those” rule.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a limited-entry decision table, how are the values of conditions and actions shown?
notes.back: As Boolean values, true or false, apart from irrelevant or infeasible ones.
notes.explanation: Every condition is reduced to a yes-or-no question.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In an extended-entry decision table, what values may conditions and actions take?
notes.back: Multiple values, for example ranges of numbers, equivalence partitions or discrete values.
notes.explanation: This lets one row carry a condition that has more than two possible answers.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table notation, what does “T” mean for a condition?
notes.back: The condition is satisfied (true).
notes.explanation: It is one of the two Boolean values a condition can take.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table notation, what does “F” mean for a condition?
notes.back: The condition is not satisfied (false).
notes.explanation: It is the opposite Boolean value to T.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table notation, what does “–” mean for a condition?
notes.back: The condition's value is irrelevant for the action outcome.
notes.explanation: Whatever the condition is, the rule's actions stay the same.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table notation, what does “N/A” mean for a condition?
notes.back: The condition is infeasible for that rule.
notes.explanation: That combination cannot occur, which is different from the condition not mattering.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table notation, what does “X” mean for an action?
notes.back: The action should occur.
notes.explanation: In a limited-entry table an action has just two values: X where it should occur and a blank where it should not.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table notation, what does a blank action cell mean?
notes.back: The action should not occur.
notes.explanation: An empty cell is itself an expected result: the action must be absent.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What makes a decision table “full”?
notes.back: It has enough columns to cover every combination of conditions.
notes.explanation: Nothing is left out, including combinations that cannot happen.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can a full decision table be simplified?
notes.back: By deleting columns that contain infeasible combinations of conditions.
notes.explanation: Combinations that cannot occur need no test.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can a decision table be minimised?
notes.back: By merging into one column those columns that differ only in conditions that do not change the outcome.
notes.explanation: Merging leaves fewer rules to exercise without losing any distinct outcome.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are decision table minimisation algorithms part of the Foundation syllabus?
notes.back: No; they are out of scope.
notes.explanation: Candidates need to know that tables can be minimised, not the algorithms for doing it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In decision table testing, what are the coverage items?
notes.back: The columns containing feasible combinations of conditions.
notes.explanation: Infeasible columns are left out because no test could exercise them.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is decision table coverage measured?
notes.back: Exercised columns divided by the total number of feasible columns, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: 100% therefore means every feasible column has been exercised.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the strength of decision table testing?
notes.back: It works through every combination of conditions methodically, so combinations that are easy to forget are not missed.
notes.explanation: Listing every combination leaves no room for a forgotten case to slip by.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides combinations, what else does decision table testing help find in requirements?
notes.back: Gaps or contradictions.
notes.explanation: A column with no agreed outcome, or with two conflicting ones, points to a problem in the requirements.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why can exercising every decision rule be time-consuming when there are many conditions?
notes.back: The number of rules grows exponentially with the number of conditions.
notes.explanation: Each extra condition multiplies, rather than adds to, the number of combinations.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two ways to reduce the number of decision rules that need to be exercised?
notes.back: Use a minimised decision table, or a risk-based approach.
notes.explanation: Both trade completeness for a number of tests the team can afford.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a state diagram, what initiates a transition?
notes.back: An event, sometimes with a guard condition that must also hold.
notes.explanation: The event is the trigger; the guard condition, if any, narrows when it applies.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How long are transitions in a state diagram assumed to take?
notes.back: No time: they are assumed to be instantaneous.
notes.explanation: The model has no in-between states while a transition happens.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides changing state, what may a transition sometimes result in?
notes.back: The software taking an action.
notes.explanation: Actions are optional parts of a transition, shown after a slash in its label.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The common transition label syntax is {{c1::event [guard condition] / action}}.
notes.back: event [guard condition] / action
notes.explanation: The event comes first, any guard condition follows in square brackets, and any action follows the slash.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When can the guard condition and the action be left out of a transition label?
notes.back: When they do not exist or are irrelevant for the tester.
notes.explanation: Only the event is always needed in the label.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What did the v4.0.1 syllabus rename the “state transition diagram”?
notes.back: The state diagram, the common name for this model in computer science.
notes.explanation: The change also keeps the name consistent with the Model-Based Testing syllabus.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 10 Appendix C – Release Notes, p. 73
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a state table, what do the rows and columns represent?
notes.back: Rows represent states; columns represent events, together with guard conditions if they exist.
notes.explanation: Each state–event pair then has exactly one cell.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a cell of a state table contain?
notes.back: A transition: its target state and the resulting actions, if defined.
notes.explanation: Reading a cell answers “from this state, on this event, where do we go and what happens?”
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a state table represent invalid transitions?
notes.back: As empty cells.
notes.explanation: Every state–event pair has a cell, so the pairs with no valid transition are visible as blanks.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is a test case based on a state diagram or state table usually represented?
notes.back: As a series of events that drives the system through a series of state changes, with any actions needed.
notes.explanation: The test drives the system through the model one event at a time.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does one state transition test case usually cover just one transition?
notes.back: No; a single test case normally passes through several transitions.
notes.explanation: A sequence of events naturally passes through several transitions on its way.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many state transition coverage criteria does the v4.0.1 syllabus discuss?
notes.back: Three, out of many that exist: all states, valid transitions and all transitions coverage.
notes.explanation: Each asks more of the tests than the one before it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must tests for 100% all transitions coverage do with invalid transitions?
notes.back: Attempt to execute them, as well as exercising all the valid transitions.
notes.explanation: Checking that forbidden moves are refused is part of this criterion.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is all transitions coverage measured?
notes.back: Valid and invalid transitions exercised or attempted, divided by the total number of valid and invalid transitions, as a percentage.
notes.explanation: Invalid transitions count in both the top and the bottom of the fraction.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why should a single test case attempt only one invalid transition?
notes.back: It helps to avoid defect masking.
notes.explanation: If one invalid attempt goes wrong, a second attempt in the same test might never get a fair try.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why is all states coverage weaker than valid transitions coverage?
notes.back: Every state can usually be reached without taking every transition.
notes.explanation: Reaching every state says nothing about every route between states.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does full valid transitions coverage guarantee full all states coverage?
notes.back: Yes.
notes.explanation: Exercising every valid transition passes through the states those transitions connect.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does full all transitions coverage guarantee?
notes.back: Full all states coverage and full valid transitions coverage.
notes.explanation: It includes every valid transition, and more, so the weaker criteria are met along the way.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which state transition coverage criterion is the most widely used?
notes.back: Valid transitions coverage.
notes.explanation: It exercises every allowed move without requiring attempts at forbidden ones.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For what kind of software should all transitions coverage be a minimum requirement?
notes.back: Mission-critical and safety-critical software.
notes.explanation: Where failure is most costly, the syllabus sets the strongest of its three criteria as the floor.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester reads a function's source code and designs tests so that every line of it runs. Which category of test technique is this?
notes.back: White-box.
notes.choices:
A) Black-box
B) White-box
C) Experience-based
notes.choicesExplained: A: black-box techniques work from specified behaviour, not from the code. C: the tests come from the code's structure, not from the tester's past experience.
notes.explanation: The tests are designed from the internal structure of the code.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester designs tests for a mortgage calculator using only its written requirements and never looks at its code. Which category of test technique is this?
notes.back: Black-box.
notes.choices:
A) Black-box
B) White-box
C) Experience-based
notes.choicesExplained: B: white-box techniques need the internal structure, which the tester never saw. C: the tests come from written requirements, not from the tester's experience.
notes.explanation: The tests rest on specified behaviour, with no reference to internal structure.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A senior tester plans tests for a new payroll screen around the failures she has seen in three earlier payroll systems. Which category of test technique is this?
notes.back: Experience-based.
notes.choices:
A) Black-box
B) White-box
C) Experience-based
notes.choicesExplained: A: no specification is being analysed. B: no internal structure is being analysed.
notes.explanation: The tests come from the tester's own knowledge and experience.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team rewrites its tax module in a new programming language. The required behaviour is unchanged. Which tests are still useful as they stand?
notes.back: The black-box tests, because they depend on required behaviour, not on the implementation.
notes.choices:
A) The black-box tests
B) The white-box tests
C) Neither kind
notes.choicesExplained: B: white-box tests depend on how the software is designed, and that design has changed. C: black-box tests stay useful when behaviour is unchanged.
notes.explanation: Only the implementation changed, and black-box test cases never referred to it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A project has finished its requirements but has no design or code yet. Which category of test technique cannot yet be used to create test cases?
notes.back: White-box.
notes.choices:
A) Black-box
B) White-box
C) Neither: both can be used now
notes.choicesExplained: A: black-box tests need only the specified behaviour, which the requirements give. C: white-box tests have no structure to work from yet.
notes.explanation: White-box test cases can only be created after the design or implementation exists.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A suite built with equivalence partitioning and statement-level code tests passes cleanly. A manager asks whether an experienced tester's session could still find anything. What does the syllabus suggest?
notes.back: Yes: experience-based techniques can find defects that black-box and white-box techniques may miss.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it may find defects the other techniques missed
B) No, systematic techniques leave nothing to find
C) Only if the code has changed
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus says experience-based techniques can detect defects the others miss. C: the value does not depend on code changes.
notes.explanation: That is why the syllabus calls them complementary.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A test suite exercises 36 of the 48 coverage items a technique identified. What is its coverage?
notes.explanation: Coverage is the share of identified coverage items exercised: 36 ÷ 48.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “coverage”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The degree to which specified coverage items are exercised by a test suite, expressed as a percentage.

notes.front: A gym app accepts membership lengths from 1 to 24 whole months. Using equivalence partitioning alone, what partitions does this input have?
notes.back: Three: below 1 (invalid), 1 to 24 (valid) and above 24 (invalid).
notes.explanation: Every value from 1 to 24 should be handled alike; values on either side should all be rejected.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A courier weighs parcels to the nearest 0.1 kg. It charges one rate for 0.1–2.0 kg, another for 2.1–10.0 kg, and rejects 0 kg or less and anything over 10.0 kg. What is the minimum number of tests for 100% EP coverage?
notes.back: Four: one each for 0 or less, 0.1–2.0, 2.1–10.0 and over 10.0 kg.
notes.explanation: EP coverage needs one test in every partition, the two invalid ones included.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A partition of valid values runs from 1 to 9. The tester has already tested 5. A colleague wants to add 3, 6 and 8. Does EP call for them?
notes.back: No; under EP one test per partition is sufficient.
notes.choices:
A) No, one value per partition is enough
B) Yes, EP needs at least three values per partition
C) Yes, but only 8, the largest value
notes.choicesExplained: B: EP asks for one test per partition. C: EP gives no reason to prefer 8, which is not even the partition's edge; that is 9.
notes.explanation: If 5 behaves correctly, EP expects every other value in the partition to behave the same.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester identifies six partitions, two of them invalid. The tests exercise only the four valid ones. What is the EP coverage?
notes.back: About 67% (4 of 6), because invalid partitions count towards coverage.
notes.explanation: 100% EP coverage needs every identified partition, invalid ones included.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For a ticket price, a tester defines the partitions “ages 0 to 18” and “ages 18 to 65”. What is wrong?
notes.back: They overlap at 18, and equivalence partitions must not overlap.
notes.choices:
A) They overlap at 18
B) They are too wide to be partitions
C) Ages cannot be partitioned
notes.choicesExplained: B: the syllabus sets no width limit on partitions. C: ages are ordered data and can be partitioned.
notes.explanation: Age 18 would belong to two partitions, so no single expected treatment applies to it.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A specification says usernames must be 3 to 20 characters and longer ones are rejected. Which kind of partition holds a 25-character username?
notes.back: An invalid partition.
notes.choices:
A) A valid partition
B) An invalid partition
C) No partition; it is a boundary value
notes.choicesExplained: A: valid partitions hold values the test object should process. C: 25 is inside the partition of lengths over 20, not at its edge, and in any case boundary values belong to partitions.
notes.explanation: The specification says such values should be rejected.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A sign-up form has “account type” (personal, business, charity) and “payment method” (card, transfer, cheque, direct debit). What is the minimum number of tests for Each Choice coverage?
notes.back: Four.
notes.explanation: Each test covers one partition from each set, so the larger set, with four partitions, sets the minimum.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The sign-up tests reach Each Choice coverage. A manager asks whether “charity paying by cheque” has been tested. What can the tester say?
notes.back: Not necessarily: Each Choice coverage does not take combinations of partitions into account.
notes.choices:
A) Not necessarily: combinations are not required
B) Yes: Each Choice covers every combination
C) Yes: cheque is a partition, so every pairing with it is covered
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: Each Choice needs each partition once, not each combination of partitions.
notes.explanation: A suite can use every account type and every payment method without ever pairing those two.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 Equivalence Partitioning, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which input can boundary value analysis be applied to?
notes.back: Number of guests, 1 to 12.
notes.choices:
A) Favourite colour, chosen from a list
B) Number of guests, 1 to 12
C) Country of birth
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: colours and countries have no natural order, so their partitions have no minimum or maximum.
notes.explanation: BVA needs ordered partitions, and only this input is ordered.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A partition of passing exam marks runs from 40 to 69, in whole marks. What are its boundary values?
notes.explanation: A partition's boundary values are its minimum and maximum.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hotel accepts stays of 1 to 14 whole nights. Using 2-value BVA, which values are the coverage items?
notes.explanation: Each boundary (1 and 14) is paired with its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition (0 and 15).
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A kettle's temperature setting accepts 40 to 100 whole degrees. Using 3-value BVA, which values are the coverage items?
notes.explanation: Each boundary (40 and 100) is taken with both its neighbours.

notes.front: 2-value BVA identifies 8 boundary values. The tests exercise 6 of them. What is the coverage?
notes.explanation: Coverage is boundary values exercised over boundary values identified: 6 ÷ 8.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40

notes.front: A discount should apply from 5 items upward, but the developer coded it for multiples of 5 only. At the boundary 5, 2-value BVA tries 4 and 5. Do they reveal the defect, and which 3-value BVA value would?
notes.back: No; 4 and 5 both behave correctly. 6, the extra 3-value neighbour, gets no discount and exposes it.
notes.explanation: The faulty rule and the correct one agree at 4 and 5 and first differ at 6.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Free delivery should start at £50.00, but the shop only grants it from £50.01. What kind of defect is this?
notes.back: A misplaced boundary, the typical kind BVA finds.
notes.choices:
A) A misplaced boundary
B) A missing partition
C) A defect only white-box testing can find
notes.choicesExplained: B: the partitions exist; only their edge is in the wrong place. C: BVA, a black-box technique, targets exactly this kind of defect.
notes.explanation: The implemented boundary sits just above its intended position.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A loan rule has three conditions, each true or false. How many columns does a full limited-entry decision table have?
notes.explanation: A full table has a column for every combination of conditions.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A table has the conditions “age under 18” and “age over 65”. One column has both true. What should the tester do with it?
notes.back: Mark it infeasible (N/A) and delete the column to simplify the table.
notes.choices:
A) Mark it infeasible and delete the column
B) Keep it and write a test for it
C) Mark both conditions “–”
notes.choicesExplained: B: an infeasible combination cannot be tested. C: “–” means irrelevant, not impossible.
notes.explanation: No customer can be both, so no test could exercise that column.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two columns of a decision table differ only in “loyalty member” (T in one, F in the other) and have the same actions. How can the table be minimised?
notes.back: Merge them into one column with “–” for loyalty member.
notes.explanation: The condition does not affect the outcome in those rules, so it is irrelevant there.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A full decision table has 8 columns, 2 of them infeasible. The tests exercise 3 columns. What is the decision table coverage?
notes.back: 50% (3 of 6 feasible columns).
notes.explanation: Only feasible columns are coverage items, so infeasible ones leave the total.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: While building a decision table, a tester finds the requirements say nothing about customers who are both new and overseas. Which strength of decision table testing is at work?
notes.back: It helps find gaps in the requirements.
notes.choices:
A) Finding gaps in the requirements
B) Measuring code coverage
C) Reducing the number of conditions
notes.choicesExplained: B: decision table coverage counts columns, not code. C: the table lays out conditions; it does not remove them.
notes.explanation: Listing every combination exposed one the requirements never addressed.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A pricing rule has ten true-or-false conditions, giving 1,024 decision rules. What can the team do to cut the number of rules to exercise?
notes.back: Use a minimised decision table or a risk-based approach.
notes.explanation: These are the two ways the syllabus names for handling exponential growth.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A decision table has the condition “order value” with the entries “under £20”, “£20–£100” and “over £100”. What kind of table is it?
notes.back: Extended-entry.
notes.choices:
A) Limited-entry
B) Extended-entry
C) State table
notes.choicesExplained: A: limited-entry tables use only true and false. C: a state table has states and events, not conditions and actions.
notes.explanation: A condition that takes several values, here ranges, marks an extended-entry table.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Members always get free delivery; non-members get it only on orders over £40. Using a full decision table of both conditions, how many tests give 100% decision table coverage?
notes.back: Four: every combination of “member” and “order over £40” is feasible.
notes.explanation: Two true-or-false conditions make four columns, and none is infeasible.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A document moves Draft → Submitted (submit), Submitted → Draft (reject), Submitted → Approved (approve) and Approved → Published (publish). What is the fewest test cases for 100% all states coverage?
notes.back: One: submit, approve, publish visits all four states.
notes.explanation: A single sequence of events can pass through every state.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the same document workflow (submit, reject, approve, publish), what single test case gives 100% valid transitions coverage?
notes.back: Submit, reject, submit, approve, publish.
notes.explanation: That sequence exercises all four valid transitions, reject included.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the document workflow, the test “submit, approve, publish” reaches every state. What valid transitions coverage does it give?
notes.back: 75%: three of the four valid transitions; reject is never exercised.
notes.explanation: Full all states coverage was reached without exercising every transition.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The document workflow's state table has 4 states and 4 events, with 4 valid transitions. How many coverage items does all transitions coverage have?
notes.back: 16: the 4 valid transitions and the 12 invalid ones (empty cells).
notes.explanation: All transitions coverage counts every cell of the state table.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: One test tries “publish” on a Draft document and then “approve” on it. The first attempt is wrongly accepted. Why is this test poorly designed?
notes.back: It attempts two invalid transitions; the first defect can mask the second.
notes.choices:
A) Two invalid transitions in one test risk defect masking
B) Invalid transitions should never be tested
C) It should start from the Published state
notes.choicesExplained: B: all transitions coverage requires attempting invalid transitions. C: the start state is not the problem; combining invalid attempts is.
notes.explanation: Testing one invalid transition per test case helps avoid defect masking.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A transition is labelled “withdraw [balance ≥ amount] / dispense cash”. Which part is the guard condition?
notes.back: balance ≥ amount.
notes.choices:
A) withdraw
B) balance ≥ amount
C) dispense cash
notes.choicesExplained: A: “withdraw” is the event. C: “dispense cash” is the action.
notes.explanation: The label follows event [guard condition] / action.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the document workflow's state table, the cell for state Published and event reject is empty. What does that mean?
notes.back: Reject from Published is an invalid transition.
notes.choices:
A) It is an invalid transition
B) The transition is valid but has no action
C) The tester forgot to fill it in
notes.choicesExplained: B: a valid transition would show its target state in the cell. C: empty cells are the table's way of showing invalid transitions.
notes.explanation: A state table shows invalid transitions as empty cells.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team tests the state model of railway signalling software. What should be its minimum state transition coverage criterion?
notes.back: All transitions coverage.
notes.choices:
A) All states coverage
B) Valid transitions coverage
C) All transitions coverage
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: both are weaker, and neither tries the invalid transitions.
notes.explanation: The syllabus sets it as a minimum for mission- and safety-critical software.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester writes one state transition test: submit, reject, submit, approve. How many transitions does it cover?
notes.back: Four transitions, three of them distinct (submit twice, reject, approve).
notes.explanation: One test case is a sequence of events and usually covers several transitions.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A requirement lists how a mix of “new customer”, “order over £100” and “paid by voucher” decides which discounts apply. Which black-box technique fits it best?
notes.back: Decision table testing.
notes.choices:
A) Decision table testing
B) State transition testing
C) Boundary value analysis
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing here depends on states or sequences of events. C: BVA could test the £100 edge, but not how the three conditions combine to decide the discounts.
notes.explanation: The requirement specifies how combinations of conditions lead to different outcomes.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A thermostat moves between “off”, “heating” and “eco” modes as buttons are pressed and temperatures change. Which black-box technique fits it best?
notes.back: State transition testing, working from a state diagram.
notes.choices:
A) State transition testing
B) Equivalence partitioning
C) Decision table testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: partitions group data values, but here the behaviour depends on the current mode and the event. C: a decision table shows combinations of conditions, not sequences of states.
notes.explanation: Its behaviour depends on which state it is in and which event occurs.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a decision table for gym prices, “student?” and “off-peak?” are conditions and “apply 20% discount” is an action. Where do they go, and what does each column hold?
notes.back: All three are rows. Each column is one decision rule: a combination of the two conditions with its expected action.
notes.explanation: Conditions and actions form the rows; rules form the columns.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do black-box and white-box test techniques differ in what they analyse?
notes.back: Black-box analyses the specified behaviour; white-box analyses the test object's internal structure and processing.
notes.explanation: That difference decides when each can be used and whether code changes affect the tests.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.1 Test Techniques Overview, p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a limited-entry decision table differ from an extended-entry one?
notes.back: Limited-entry uses only true or false values; extended-entry lets conditions and actions take multiple values, such as ranges.
notes.explanation: Extended entries fit conditions that have more than two possible answers.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do 2-value and 3-value BVA differ in their coverage items per boundary?
notes.back: 2-value: the boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition. 3-value: the boundary value and both its neighbours.
notes.explanation: The third item makes 3-value BVA the more rigorous of the two.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 Boundary Value Analysis, p. 40
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a state table show explicitly that a state diagram does not?
notes.back: Invalid transitions.
notes.explanation: A diagram draws only valid transitions, while a table gives every state–event pair a cell.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does all transitions coverage differ from valid transitions coverage?
notes.back: It also attempts the invalid transitions shown in the state table, not only the valid ones.
notes.explanation: That extra demand is what makes it the stronger criterion.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4 State Transition Testing, p. 42
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a decision table, how does “–” differ from “N/A” for a condition?
notes.back: “–” means the condition is irrelevant to the outcome; “N/A” means the condition is infeasible for that rule.
notes.explanation: One marks a condition that does not matter, the other a combination that cannot happen.
notes.source: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level Syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3 Decision Table Testing, p. 41
